items.followUp: If 10 Vernier divisions equal 9 mm, write the formula for least count and calculate the least count of the Vernier calipers.

accept: value of one main scale division
rubric.why: The formula is needed to determine the instrument’s least count.
rubric.how: Award for writing least count = value of one main-scale division ÷ number of Vernier-scale divisions, or its equivalent symbolic form.

rubric.why: Gives the standard numerical least count for Vernier calipers.
rubric.description: Calculates the least count with its unit.
rubric.how: Award for the correct least-count value in either mm or cm.

modelAnswer: Formula: Least count = value of one main-scale division ÷ number of divisions on the Vernier scale.
For standard Vernier calipers, 1 main-scale division = 1 mm and the Vernier scale has 10 divisions.

items.followUp: Why is rolling friction smaller than sliding friction?

rubric.why: States the comparison between the two types of friction.
rubric.description: Compares sliding friction with rolling friction.
rubric.how: Award for stating that sliding friction is greater than rolling friction.

rubric.why: Explains the reduced rubbing and interlocking during rolling.
rubric.description: Gives the reason rolling friction is smaller.
rubric.how: Award for explaining that rolling surfaces do not continuously slide over each other, so their irregularities interlock and rub less.

modelAnswer: Sliding friction is much greater than rolling friction.
As surfaces roll, they do not continuously slide over each other; therefore, their irregularities interlock and rub less.
